summary: Postmortem follow-up for the 2026-05-12 incident where customer-facing inference requests experienced sustained errors and elevated latency. Root cause appears to be an interplay between Redwood autoscaler behavior under a burst of traffic, a model worker GPU OOM during cache warmup, and an upstream NLB health-check flapping. Discussed mitigations: hotfix to autoscaler, fallback routing to smaller model variant, dedicated canary pool, and improved observability and alerting. Action items assigned and next steps agreed.
topics: Root cause analysis (autoscaler + GPU OOM + NLB flapping)

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-15
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Taylor Morgan (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Das (Redwood CSM), Sandra Kim (Aperture VP Eng), Ravi Menon (Aperture SRE), Elena Ortiz (Aperture Security), Marcus Li (Aperture Infra)

Auto summary (auto-generated): Brief review of 2026-05-12 outage, RCA discussion, action items for logs and fixes.

[00:00] Taylor Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to go through the postmortem, uh, recap the timeline and make sure we have concrete next steps. Who wants to kick off from Aperture?
[00:18] Sandra Kim: Hi, yeah thanks. We got a bunch of customer reports friday night, high 5xx rates and threads timing out. the issue started around 18:20 UTC and about it lasted for, for like 20 minutes of elevated errors and then intermittent for the next couple hours.
[00:35] Ravi Menon: yeah the symptoms from our side were sudden spike in response lat and errors, then a rapid scale up of workers and some of them started failing health checks. we saw the NLB mark a few nodes unhealthy which then caused a reshuffle.
[00:52] Jordan Lee: On the Redwood side we saw a burst of traffic for Aperture's prod route, the autoscaler spun up additional workers, but one of the model workers hit a GPU OOM during K V cache warmup — pardon the K V cahce, um — and that worker crashed, which then caused a small cascade with the load balancer.
[01:10] Marcus Li: the timing matches our logs, we also had a config change to the NLB health check earlier friday to shorten the timeout window, that may have made flapping more likely.
[01:28] Elena Ortiz: for compliance, did any of the failed requests result in data exfil or persistent logs we need to be worried about?
[01:35] Priya Das: quick answer: no evidence of data exfil; requests were retried and some logs were generated, but we do keep full audit logs and we're happy to share the relevant slices.
[01:50] Sandra Kim: okay good. can we go through the timeline step by step?
[01:55] Taylor Morgan: absolutely. Jordan, can you read the short timeline you prepared?
[02:03] Jordan Lee: sure, so start 18:20 UTC: sustained traffic spike; 18:21 autoscaler policy triggered, attempted to launch additional GPU workers; 18:23 first worker reports GPU OOM during model kv cache populate; 18:24 worker restarts, Kubernetes liveness probe fails because the worker didn't come up in expected window; 18:25 NLB marks the pod unhealthy and removes it from rotation; 18:26 other pods get more traffic, one more OOM occurs during aggressive prefix cache population; 18:28 we saw elevated 5xx and increased latency; mitigation started 18:29 where we patched the autoscaler to be more conservative and routed a percentage of traffic to a lighter-weight model variant; by 18:36 error rates dropped back to baseline.
[03:10] Ravi Menon: question — you mentioned a hotfix to autoscaler. what was the exact change?
[03:15] Jordan Lee: we adjusted the scale-up threshold and added a cooldown period so we don't spin up too many heavy GPU workers simultaneously on very short spikes. we also added an immediate fallback policy to route new requests to an alternate compatible model (smaller profile) if the worker pool isn't stable.
[03:35] Sandra Kim: does that fallback change affect output quality for our customers? some of our use cases are quality-sensitive.
[03:41] Taylor Morgan: yes it can — fallback to a smaller model is a tradeoff. for Aperture we configured the fallback to a slightly smaller variant that we validated against your key prompts; the degradation was small on average but we documented it. we'll include sample outputs in the postmortem doc.
[03:59] Elena Ortiz: and about audit logs — will we get the exact request ids and timestamps for compliance investigations?
[04:06] Jordan Lee: yes, we have the audit slice. I'll package the request IDs and the related worker traces and send them. note that some trace segments in the moment might be missing due to process crash, but we have enough to reconstruct the sequence.
[04:24] Marcus Li: did the OOM happen only on a particular GPU type?
[04:29] Jordan Lee: looks like it was an A100 instance in the pool for Aperture. the model's KV cache warmed to an unexpectedly large prefix size due to some prompt patterns that were seen in the spike. our memory accounting underestimated the peak live set during warmup.
[04:47] Ravi Menon: interesting — we did push a new customer prompt template last week which does include longer context for the same endpoint. that might have contributed.
[04:56] Sandra Kim: right — we changed prompt length at 17:50, so that precedes the incident. ok that explains the extra memory.
[05:05] Taylor Morgan: big picture: it's a three-way issue — customer prompt change increasing context, autoscaler behavior hitting too many heavy workers at once, and NLB health-check sensitivity causing flapping. each on its own might not have caused the outage but together they cascaded.
[05:22] Priya Das: quick note — we did run a canary before the prompt change but it didn't cover the production traffic spike scenario. we'll update our canary templates to include stress patterns.
[05:35] Sandra Kim: so immediate mitigations — what did Redwood do in-prod during the incident?
[05:42] Jordan Lee: immediate steps were: 1) reduce autoscale aggressiveness (cooldown), 2) take ~30% traffic and route to smaller model variant, 3) restart the unhealthy workers with a slightly higher probe timeout, 4) temporarily pin some sessions to stable warm workers where possible.
[05:58] Marcus Li: did you do any config changes to the NLB?
[06:02] Jordan Lee: we didn't change the NLB settings in prod during the incident; we recommended to Aperture to revert the recent shorter health-check window.
[06:10] Sandra Kim: we'll revert that now and monitor.
[06:14] Elena Ortiz: from a security POV, is there any risk with routing to a different model variant or to a canary pool? data residency or logs separation?
[06:23] Taylor Morgan: good question — routing to a Redwood-managed smaller model stays within the same tenancy and logging policies; no cross-tenant data leakage. if you require strict separation we can use a dedicated canary pool in your VPC or a dedicated account to guarantee physical isolation.
[06:41] Sandra Kim: we'd prefer the dedicated canary pool for future tests. cost is a factor but for safety we want isolation.
[06:48] Taylor Morgan: noted. we'll propose a dedicated canary pool config and pricing.
[06:52] Ravi Menon: long term fixes — what's on Redwood's list?
[06:56] Jordan Lee: our engineering plan is: 1) fix memory accounting around KV cache warmup — patch in progress, 2) add pre-warm policy to stage partial cache during scale operations, 3) autoscaler improvements to avoid simultaneous heavy launches, 4) introduce a model-variant quality gating so fallback is smoother, 5) add better alerting for interleaved LB flapping + OOM patterns.
[07:20] Sandra Kim: timeline for the memory accounting patch?
[07:23] Jordan Lee: we're targeting a hotfix in one week (by 2026-05-22) for the accounting patch, then a follow-up rollout for pre-warm over two weeks after that.
[07:33] Taylor Morgan: on the ops side Priya will run the SLA credit process and we can talk about a partial credit depending on the severity window.
[07:41] Priya Das: yes I'll open the ticket and loop Legal if needed.
[07:45] Marcus Li: can we get more granular observability metrics? specifically per-worker GPU memory usage over time and per-request latency percentiles?
[07:54] Jordan Lee: absolutely — we already surfaced additional dashboards for Aperture; I'll share those links. the plan is to add an alert that triggers when combined signals (gpu memory > 80% + pod restarts + NLB unhealthy count) occur within a 5-minute window.
[08:12] Elena Ortiz: do we have SOC2/ISO implications here? any control failures?
[08:18] Taylor Morgan: from what we've seen, this is operational resilience rather than a security control failure. audit logs are intact; no evidence of data compromise. it should not impact SOC2 status. we'll include a note in the postmortem for your compliance team.
[08:33] Sandra Kim: good. about the fallback quality — can you share examples where fallback produced different outputs?
[08:40] Jordan Lee: yes we'll attach sample pairs of original vs fallback outputs for your key prompt set in the doc. note that in our internal checks the top-k and beam differences were minor for your workload.
[08:55] Ravi Menon: one concern — autoscaler cooldown may increase latency under real load if we are slower to add capacity. how do we balance that?
[09:03] Taylor Morgan: it's a tradeoff. the cooldown is tuned to avoid flapping; we also implemented progressive scale steps — smaller increments first, and if the spike persists we accelerate. plus the fallback to smaller model gives headroom while new workers stabilize.
[09:18] Sandra Kim: okay. for the dedicated pool option — what's the lead time?
[09:22] Taylor Morgan: for a dedicated reserved pool we can provision in 3-5 business days for common GPU types; for on-prem/VPC integration there is a 2-3 week onboarding depending on networking.
[09:35] Marcus Li: we might take the dedicated pool for peak hours to avoid shared noisy neighbor issues. can you give cost estimates?
[09:41] Taylor Morgan: yes I'll send a pricing addendum by Tue (2026-05-19).
[09:46] Sandra Kim: any customer-facing comms we need to send? we paused notices friday because we were triaging; should we send a follow-up?
[09:52] Priya Das: we recommend a short note: summary, mitigation, and assurance of follow-up with the detailed postmortem. we'll draft that and share with your comms team for approval.
[10:05] Jordan Lee: small technical note — we've got some partial traces where the process crashed before logging finished, so there are gaps; that is why we want your NLB config and the exact prompt payloads for the spike to correlate.
[10:20] Ravi Menon: we'll export and send the relevant logs by monday.
[10:24] Sandra Kim: is there any chance the issue repeats with a different model or pattern?
[10:29] Jordan Lee: possible if a combination of very long context and rapid traffic spike align. the pre-warm and better memory accounting should reduce that risk significantly.
[10:40] Taylor Morgan: ok let's recap next steps. Jordan will send traces and dashboards, I'll send pricing and dedicated pool options, Priya will open the SLA ticket and draft customer comms, Aperture (Ravi/Sandra) will send NLB and prompt payloads. we'll schedule a deeper technical session week of 2026-05-24.
[11:02] Sandra Kim: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:05] Elena Ortiz: thanks, appreciate the quick response.
[11:07] Taylor Morgan: thanks all — we'll follow up in writing by EOD Monday.
